summary: Describes a widely implemented URI scheme for referring to television broadcasts, for use in web browsers on devices like television sets and set-top boxes. It builds on the URI format in RFC 2396. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A web link normally points at a page. This makes a link that points at a TV channel, so a TV can tune to it.

questions: how do you reference a tv broadcast with a uri
what is the tv uri format
subtitle: A web link scheme for television broadcasts on network-connected devices.

tldr.problem: Web browsers are appearing on televisions and set-top boxes, but they need a way to reference and tune to television broadcasts using URI format, just as browsers reference web pages.
tldr.mechanism: The tv: URI scheme uses DNS-style identifiers to refer to television broadcasts, allowing a device to map the identifier to a local broadcast frequency or channel. The simplest form, tv:, refers to the current broadcast.
tldr.outcome: A widely-implemented URI scheme that enables web content embedded in broadcasts to link to the broadcast itself, and allows interactive television services to be built using standard web technologies.

today: RFC 2838 is an informational specification and has not been obsoleted. The tv: URI scheme remains in use in interactive television applications and set-top box browsers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
As web browsers began appearing on television sets and set-top boxes in the late 1990s, a need emerged to reference television broadcasts using the URI format already standardized in RFC 2396. This document specifies a URI scheme for television broadcasts that is widely implemented in consumer electronics.

The scheme is particularly useful for interactive television applications, where HTML content is broadcast alongside audio and video. A TV URI can link viewers from web content back to the broadcast with which the content was received, or to other broadcasts available on the local device.
sections.eli5: TVs started having web browsers like computers do. A web browser needs a way to make links that point at TV channels instead of web pages.

sections.title: The tv: URI Syntax
sections.content:
The basic structure of a television URI is the scheme name tv: followed by an optional broadcast identifier. The simplest form, tv: with no identifier, refers to whichever broadcast is currently being received by the device. This is the most common usage and is explicitly referenced in the Advanced Television Enhancement Forum specification.

When an identifier is needed, broadcasts are specified using DNS-style identifiers (domain names). Examples include tv:nbc.com for the NBC network or tv:wqed.org for a specific station. Multiple broadcast streams from the same organization are distinguished with subdomains: tv:east.hbo.com and tv:west.hbo.com for regional versions of HBO.
sections.eli5: A TV link is either empty (meaning 'the channel you're watching now') or has a network name like a domain name but for a TV station instead.

sections.title: DNS-Style Identifiers and Global Uniqueness
sections.content:
Television broadcasts have traditionally been identified by call signs assigned by national authorities (such as the FCC in the United States). However, many cable and satellite networks use simple names like CNN or HBO that are not globally unique. Both the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and the American Broadcasting Company use the identifier ABC.

The tv: scheme uses DNS-style identifiers to ensure global uniqueness. These identifiers need not match real hostnames and should not be resolved via DNS to IP addresses. Instead, they build on the existing DNS registration system to guarantee uniqueness. The domain name system's dispute resolution processes can be applied to resolve name collisions. A receiver must implement a local mapping from known DNS-style identifiers to actual broadcast frequencies or channels.
sections.eli5: To avoid confusion when different countries use the same TV station name, the system uses full domain-style names. A TV receiver looks up the name locally to find what frequency to tune to.

sections.title: Implementation and Device-Specific Mapping
sections.content:
Unlike URLs that specify an address to reach over the network, the tv: scheme is a Uniform Resource Identifier that merely names a broadcast signal. It assumes the local device has some means of mapping known identifiers to frequencies. This mapping is device-specific and browser-specific, and is outside the scope of this specification.

A variety of software systems provide this device-specific mapping, from simple channel-number lookups to frequency databases. These mapping systems can be incorporated into television sets or set-top boxes to facilitate interpretation of television URIs. The scheme is similar to the news: and file: URI schemes in that it names a resource but assumes local knowledge of how to access it.
sections.eli5: When you click a TV link, the TV doesn't connect to the Internet to find the channel. Instead, it uses a table it already has to figure out what frequency that channel broadcasts on locally.

sections.title: Obsolete Forms and Considerations
sections.content:
Earlier drafts of this specification supported other forms, now considered obsolete. Channel numbers, such as tv:4 (corresponding to 66 MHz in the United States), were allowed but are not recommended because the mapping of channel numbers to frequencies varies from country to country. This makes them unsuitable for use on a global Internet.

Similarly, bare network identifiers and call signs without domain suffixes (such as tv:abc or tv:kron) should not be used, as they do not provide the global uniqueness guarantees of DNS-style identifiers and are prone to name collision issues described in RFC 2838.
sections.eli5: Some old ways of writing TV links (using just channel numbers or plain station names) are not recommended because they don't work the same way everywhere in the world.
